question: A recent study published in the scientific journal PNAS1 reveals an alarming decline in African elephant populations in most of the continent. The data, covering 1964 to 2016, shows that elephants are surviving mainly in protected areas, with a dramatic reduction in forest elephants. The savannah species has almost completely disappeared from the Sahel and has declined by up to 70 % in other regions.
In 2021, the IUCN raised the threat level of the African savannah elephant to ‘endangered’ and classified the African forest elephant as ‘critically endangered’. 1.

In the context of CITES, is the Commission advocating the inclusion of all African elephants in Appendix I and opposing attempts to ensure that any elephant population is relegated from Appendix I to Appendix II?

Given that poaching to supply the ivory trade is the main cause of this decline, in what way is the Commission supporting the closure under CITES of all remaining legal national ivory markets and what is the Commission doing to oppose all proposals to lift restrictions on the trade in ivory?
Survey-based inference of continental African elephant decline.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.1.2025) The study is an analysis of the already available data from 1964-2016. The Commission is aware of this data, which shows that global elephant densities are decreasing. The data shows also that densities in some populations, especially of L. africana in southern African countries were increasing.

These are the countries where sustainable management forms an integral part of elephant conservation. The study did not include the most recent available population data for L. africana from Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe from 2022 (Bussière & Potgieter 2023), which harbour about 50% of all African elephants and which confirmed a stable population in this region.

The African elephants are currently listed in App. I, while some populations from southern Africa are listed in App. II, which allows conservation and management interventions appropriate to the conservation needs of specific populations.

Furthermore, discussion is ongoing within the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES)1 on changing the standard nomenclature for elephants, accepting L. cyclotis as separate species.

In the process of the preparation of the upcoming meeting of the Conference of Parties to CITES, the Commission will carefully analyse any proposals, including those related to trade in African elephants, and propose to the Council of the European Union an evidence-based and proportionate EU position.
